To broil means to cook food using direct, intense heat. The key word here is direct — the heat doesn't surround the food from all sides (the way an oven bakes bread); it blasts at the food from one direction, typically from above, at a very high temperature. This intense, focused heat rapidly browns, chars, and crisps the outer surface of the food while cooking the inside.

Picture a thick steak placed just a few inches below a glowing-red heating element in an oven, with the surface turning dark and caramelized in minutes. That's broiling.

When you broil in an oven, you switch the oven to its "broil" setting, which activates a heating element at the top of the oven. You place the food on a rack positioned close to that element — usually 3 to 6 inches away. The food is then bombarded by radiant heat from directly above.

Because the heat is so intense and direct, broiling:

  • Browns and chars the surface quickly
  • Creates a slightly crispy, caramelized outer layer
  • Is best suited for thin or flat pieces of food (fish fillets, chicken breasts, burgers, vegetables), since thick items might burn on the outside before the inside cooks through
  • Requires close attention — food can go from perfectly browned to burnt in under a minute

You would say:

  • "Broil the salmon for 5 minutes until the top is golden."
  • "She broiled the chicken thighs under the heating element."
Broiling vs. similar cooking methods — knowing the difference

Understanding broiling becomes clearer when you compare it to related cooking words:

Broil vs. Grill
This is the most important comparison. In everyday American English, these two words describe the same kind of cooking (direct, high heat, browning the surface), but from opposite directions:

  • Grill → heat comes from below (like a barbecue or stovetop grill pan, with flames or a grate beneath the food)
  • Broil → heat comes from above (the heating element at the top of the oven)

The results are very similar — both give you a browned, slightly charred surface — but the setup is different. This is why Americans say "broil it in the oven" and "grill it on the barbecue."

(Note for British English speakers: In the UK, what Americans call "broiling" is simply called "grilling." A British recipe that says "grill the fish under a hot element" means the same thing as an American recipe that says "broil the fish." Americans use the word "grill" almost exclusively for outdoor cooking over a flame or charcoal.)

Broil vs. Bake/Roast

  • When you bake or roast, the heat in the oven surrounds the food from all sides — it's indirect and enveloping. The food cooks slowly and evenly throughout.
  • When you broil, only the top surface faces the heat. It's fast, fierce, and one-directional.

This is why people sometimes broil a dish for the last few minutes after baking it — to give it a golden, browned top that baking alone wouldn't produce. For example: a casserole is baked until cooked through, then broiled briefly so the cheese on top bubbles and browns.

Broil vs. Fry

  • Fry means cooking in hot oil or fat.
  • Broil uses no oil or fat at all — just dry, radiant heat. It's actually considered a relatively healthy cooking method for this reason.

Broil vs. Sear

  • Sear means to brown the surface of food at very high heat (usually on a stovetop pan). The goal — browning the surface — is similar, but searing is done in a pan, often with a little oil, while broiling is done in an oven with dry heat from above.
Figurative use: "to broil" meaning to be intensely hot

Beyond cooking, broil is also used figuratively to describe a person or thing suffering under extreme heat — as if they were being cooked:

  • "We broiled in the summer heat waiting for the bus."
  • "Tourists were broiling on the beach under the midday sun."
  • "The workers broiled on the rooftop all afternoon."

In this sense, the verb simply expresses the feeling of being subjected to unbearable, intense heat. You're not literally cooking, but the analogy makes the discomfort vivid and relatable.
Rare/archaic use: "to broil" meaning to be in turmoil

In older literature and formal writing, broil occasionally appears with a completely different meaning: to be in a state of fierce conflict, agitation, or disorder. You might encounter this in classic novels or historical texts:

  • "The court broiled with intrigue and betrayal."
  • "The city broiled in civil unrest."

This usage is largely obsolete in modern everyday English. If you encounter it in a novel written before the 20th century, it means the situation is chaotic, turbulent, or caught up in strife. You do not need to use this sense yourself; knowing it exists is enough.
Summary of all uses at a glance

1. Primary meaning (cooking): To cook food under direct, high, dry heat from above, typically using an oven's broil setting. The surface browns and chars quickly.
  2. Figurative meaning: To be exposed to intense heat; to swelter. "We broiled in the sun."
  3. Archaic meaning: To be in a state of turmoil or conflict. Rarely used today.

When you see or hear the word "broil" in modern life, it almost always refers to either the cooking method or the experience of extreme heat. The cooking sense is by far the most common.
